[Margin, p. 333: Knot IX. That God is not mutable from this, that he could found [condere] another world.]
Andab. Non eam inficias esse nodum vere Gordianum, ipsum me per non exiguum temporis districtum & trepidabundum {?distinuisse}.

Andab. I do not deny [non … inficias] it to be a knot truly Gordian, [and that it] held [{?distinuisse}, for detinuisse] me myself, distracted [districtum] and trembling [trepidabundum], through no small [space] of time.

Sed postquam animadverti Dei voluntatem aeque atque intellectum ad omnium possibilium amorem distincte pro naturarum ipsarum modo, se extendere, diluxit & illud, volitionem efficacem creandi non addere quicquam posse communi Dei volitioni, praeter entitatem ipsam factam ut terminantem amorem quem Deus versus creaturas essentialiter habet.

But after I noticed that the will of God, equally as [aeque atque] the understanding [intellectum], extends itself to the love of all possibles distinctly according to the mode of the natures themselves, that too dawned [diluxit] [on me]: that the efficacious volition [volitionem efficacem] of creating can add nothing to the common volition [communi … volitioni] of God, except the entity [entitatem] itself made, as terminating [terminantem] the love which God has essentially toward creatures.

Extrinsecam vero terminationem quantumvis varietur, intrinsecam mutabilitatem inducere nemo tam bliteus sit ut suspicetur. Exemplum habemus in cottidiana Animarum rationalium ad formationem corporum creatione, quam inducere cottidianam Deo mutationem nemo barbatorum illorum asserat.

But that an extrinsic termination [terminationem], however much it be varied, induces an intrinsic mutability, no one would be so insipid [bliteus] as to suspect. We have an example in the daily creation of rational Souls for the formation of bodies, which no one of those bearded [men] [barbatorum] would assert induces a daily change [mutationem] in God.
Ereu. Acute, Ita me Deus amet, Andabata, sed quod a te expectare sine miraculo ausim, prodidisti. Verum ego cur minus assentior, duo faciunt.

Ereu. Sharply [acute], so may God love me, Andabata — but [only] what I would dare to expect from you without a miracle — you have brought forth [prodidisti]. But why I assent less, two [things] cause [faciunt].

In nostris siquidem voluntatibus intime experimur contineri ipsum effectum quem volumus usque ad ultimam circumstantiam quam volumus. Verear itaque ne denudatam & mutilam Deo volitionem praeparemus, nisi ipsam determinationem qua haec creatura caeteris praeeligitur, ipsi intimo affectui infigamus.

For in our wills we experience inwardly [intime] that the very effect which we will is contained [in them], down to the last circumstance which we will. I would fear therefore lest we prepare for God a stripped and mutilated volition, unless we fix [infigamus] in the inmost affection [affectui] itself the very determination by which this creature is chosen before [praeeligitur] the others.
Aliud est quod existens praeter ipsum Deum universo nihil praestituamus, neque effectum aliquem nisi a causa existente sperari posse tumetipse paulo superius affirmasti.

The other is that we set before [praestituamus] the universe nothing existing besides God himself, and you yourself affirmed a little above that no effect can be hoped for except from an existing cause.

Mundum itaque, hoc est, unam possibilium particulam caeteris praeferri, causam habet antequam mundus existit saltem, ut loquuntur, natura prius. Hoc autem in terminationem aliquam extrinsecam referri non potest, terminatio enim vel posterior est creatura, vel cum ipsa coniuncta; causa autem natura saltem prior est effectu.

That the world therefore, that is, one little part [particulam] of the possibles, is preferred to the others, has a cause before the world exists — at least, as they say, prior by nature [natura prius]. But this cannot be referred to some extrinsic termination; for the termination is either posterior to the creature, or conjoined with it; but the cause is at least prior by nature to the effect.

Intra Deum itaque collocanda est haec determinatio, in voluntate proinde divina, vel sicubi alibi posueris, eodem recidet: semper enim de ea verum erit potuisse non esse; etsi potuit non esse, inferetur semper mutabilem esse Deum quandoquidem aliud esse potuerit.

Within God therefore this determination is to be placed: in the divine will accordingly, or, if you place [it] anywhere else, it will fall back [recidet] to the same [point]: for it will always be true of it that it could have not been; and if [etsi, read et si] it could not be, it will always be inferred that God is mutable, since something other [aliud] could have been.

Andab. Non ignoro militare quae dicis contra hanc sententiam. Verum hoc experior, eadem in omnes sententias stringi, & hanc solutionem paucioribus quam caeteras subiici incommodis. Videamus vero num tu liquidius, vel meracius quicquam propines.

Andab. I am not ignorant that what you say fights [militare] against this opinion [sententiam]. But this I experience: that the same [weapons] are drawn [stringi] against all opinions, and that this solution is subjected to fewer inconveniences [incommodis] than the others. But let us see whether you may pour out [propines] anything clearer [liquidius] or purer [meracius].
Ereu. Non ausim quod placeat, polliceri, sed quale, quale est, sic accipe, putasne mutabilem posse dici Deum, ex eo praecise quod plura possit, quamdiu in potentia plura illa sunt.

Ereu. I would not dare to promise what may please, but such as it is [quale, quale est], so receive [it]: do you think God can be called mutable precisely from this, that he can [do] more [things] [plura], as long as those more [things] are in potency [in potentia].
Andab. Neutiquam, modo ne potentia exiliant, verum quorsum sunt in potentia, plura, si semper in potentia futura sunt?
Andab. By no means, provided only [modo ne] they do not leap out of potency; but to what end [quorsum] are more [things] in potency, if they are always going to be in potency?

Ereu. Ne sollicitus sis: Suppositiones enim loquimur, non res. Rursus itaque si uno facto, toti potentiae satisfit, ita ut supposito quod unum factum sit, reliqua fieri neque possint neque debeant: per hoc autem mutatio nulla accidat: numquid mutabilis dicetur aliter quam quia plura possit?

Ereu. Do not be anxious: for we speak suppositions [suppositiones], not things. Again therefore, if by one [thing] made the whole potency is satisfied, so that, it being supposed that one [thing] has been made, the rest neither can nor ought to be made; and through this no change [mutatio] happens: will he be called mutable at all [numquid] otherwise than because he can [do] more [things]?

Andab. Post factum non dicetur mutabilis propter alia quae sunt in potentia, quoniam iam non sunt in potentia, postquam potentiae satisfactum est, non magis quam quilibet effectus qui semel exiuit e potentia suae causae, amplius in ea est. Non ergo ratione illorum mutabilis erit.

Andab. After the deed [post factum] he will not be called mutable on account of the other [things] which are in potency, since they are now not in potency, after the potency has been satisfied — no more than any effect which has once gone out from the potency of its cause is any longer in it. Not therefore by reason of those will he be mutable.

Ereu. Conspicare modo, Dei causam sic se habere. Potest quidem plura, sed pure posse plura, non est mutabilitas aliqua. Deinde potentia talis est ut unico actu saturetur, sicut vides totum genus electivorum sese habere; Cum enim ex pluribus unum eligere nata sunt, necesse iis est & plura posse & uno saturari.

Ereu. Behold only [conspicare modo] that God’s case [causam] holds itself thus. He can indeed [do] more [things], but purely to be able [to do] more is not any mutability. Then the potency is such that it is sated [saturetur] by a single act, as you see the whole kind of electives [electivorum] holds itself; for since they are born [nata sunt] to choose one out of more, it is necessary for them both to be able [to do] more and to be sated by one.

Rursus exitus in actum mutationem non arguit. Ea ipsa enim qua est aeternitate, eadem in actum exit, neque prius est quam actu sit. Et quod unicum fortasse tibi stomachum moveat, Unica est via qua in actum exeat, seu ad actum sese determinet. Unde sic potest plura, ut determinatio ex ipsa Dei natura supra unum tantum cadere possit. Nullus itaque mutabilitati locus est super.

Again, the going-out [exitus] into act does not argue a change. For by that very eternity by which it is, by the same it goes out into act, nor is it before it is in act. And — what alone [unicum] perhaps may move your stomach — single [unica] is the way by which it may go out into act, or determine itself to act. Whence it can [do] more [things] in such a way that the determination, from the very nature of God, can fall upon one only. No place therefore is left over [est super] for mutability.
Andab. Sed adhuc superat ea difficultas quae omnes superat, & est quod possit plura, & si possit ponatur facere aliquod aliud, non eo ipso alia erit voluntas alius Deus?

Andab. But there still remains [superat] that difficulty which surpasses [superat] all, and it is that he can [do] more [things]; and if, [since] he can, he be supposed [ponatur] to make something other, will not by that very [fact] the will be other, God other?

Ereu. Ponatur fecisse, nihil nego, quod inde colligas: sed suppositionem non concedo. Aliae enim sunt leges potentiae divinae, aliae voluntatis; per quam vel certe sine qua potentia non exit in actum.

Ereu. Let it be supposed that he has made [it]: I deny nothing which you may gather thence; but the supposition I do not grant. For other are the laws of the divine potency, other [those] of the will — through which, or certainly without which, the potency does not go out into act.

Neque hoc praeiudicat potentiae: sicut Arti Grammaticae vel Musicae non praeiudicaret quod ex aliqua causa homo non vellet, vel etiam non posset velle iis uti. Non enim propterea minus Grammaticus aut Musicus foret, vel minus posset: & tamen suppositio illa (pone factum) homini illi repugnaret, non ex defectu potentiae, sed ex accidenti.

Nor does this prejudice [praeiudicat] the potency: as it would not prejudice the Art of Grammar or of Music that from some cause a man would not will, or even could not will, to use them. For not on that account would he be less a Grammarian or Musician, or be less able: and yet that supposition (suppose [it] done [pone factum]) would be repugnant [repugnaret] to that man, not from a defect of potency, but from an accident [ex accidenti].

Habet itaque Deus potentiam ad ea quae nunquam creaturus est, qualem homo explicatus Grammaticam vel Musicam. Et cum hac potentia consistit quod nunquam usurus sit, neque possit fieri ut utatur. Et quoniam mutabilitas est possibilitas actus in mutabili, cum nulla talis possibilitas existat, neque mutabilitas ulla est.

God therefore has a potency for those [things] which he is never going to create, such as an accomplished [explicatus] man [has as] Grammar or Music. And with this potency it is consistent [consistit] that he is never going to use [it], nor can it come about that he use [it]. And since mutability is the possibility of act in the mutable, since no such possibility exists, neither is there any mutability.
Andab. Qualem nobis potentiam fingis, quae cum ad plura sit, unicum actum habere possit? At nosti axioma, frustra esse potentiam quae nunquam reducitur ad actum.

Andab. What kind of potency do you feign [fingis] for us, which, though it is for more [things], can have a single act? But you know the axiom, that a potency which is never reduced to act is in vain.

Ereu. Effatum tuum in iis potentiis fortasse valet, quae veram rationem potentiae habent, & propter actus suos sunt: quantumvis in electivis fallit. Si enim electio optima semper fiat propter quam potentia maxime facta est (& non propter alias nisi per defectum ipsius) & qua potentia optime exercetur, sequiores actus nunquam erunt. Neque propterea incassum est potentia.

Ereu. Your pronouncement [effatum] perhaps holds in those potencies which have the true notion [rationem] of potency, and are for the sake of their acts; however much [quantumvis] it fails in electives. For if the best choice is always made — for the sake of which the potency was made most of all (and not for the sake of others except through a defect of it) — and by which the potency is best exercised, the worse [sequiores] acts will never be. Nor on that account is the potency in vain.
Deus autem potentia per Analogiam quam aequivocationem ex consilio appellant, nominatur, neque ad actum ullum extra se dicitur.

But God is named [by the name of] potency [potentia] through Analogy, which they call equivocation from deliberation [aequivocationem ex consilio], nor is he said [dicitur] in relation to [ad] any act outside himself.

Asphal. Haeret etiam mihi aliquis scrupulus: De actibus enim extra Deum, id est, effectis, esto quod dixisti, sed de actibus suis internis qui ipsa sunt eius essentia, & aequales ipsi; quomodo dicis aequivocam esse rationem potentiae, & non ad eos esse institutam quam in Deo agnoscimus potentiam?

Asphal. There sticks also in me some scruple: for concerning the acts outside God, that is, the effects, be it what you have said; but concerning his internal acts, which are his very essence, and equal to him — how do you say that the notion [rationem] of potency is equivocal, and that the potency which we acknowledge in God is not instituted [institutam] in relation to them [ad eos]?

Ereu. Hic nobis ad Andabatam tanquam ad aram & asylum confugere opportunum foret, & fateri actus divinos ad quaecumque obiecta terminantur, non propterea plures esse, quoniam una est omnium essentia; termini autem materiale quidpiam, quibus mutatis, essentia actus non mutatur.

Ereu. Here it would be opportune for us to flee for refuge to Andabata as to an altar and asylum, and to confess that the divine acts, to whatever objects they are terminated, are not on that account more [than one] [plures], since the essence of all is one; but the terms [termini] [are] something material, which being changed, the essence of the act is not changed.

Quoniam tamen cum de actibus intrinsecis est sermo, extra voluntatem non proceditur, voluntas autem maxime in Deo intellectum ipsis vestigiis assequitur, intellectus etiam divinus dumtaxat demonstrative fertur; demonstrationis autem semita praecise ad unum actum voluntatis fert terminatum ad unum obiectum extrinsecum, Potentiam quae est ad actus extrinsecos ad plures esse; sed illam quae ad actus intrinsecos dicitur, ad unicum dici constabit, & hanc voluntatem esse illam potentiam creativam, seu essentiae eminentiam quae ad actus suos non dicitur; cum voluntas suae compar sit.

Since however, when the discourse is about intrinsic acts, one does not proceed outside the will, and the will, most of all in God, follows [assequitur] the understanding in its very footsteps, and the divine understanding too is borne [fertur] only demonstratively, and the path of demonstration bears [fert] precisely to one act of the will terminated at one extrinsic object: it will stand established [constabit] that the potency which is for extrinsic acts is for more [than one]; but that that which is said [in relation] to intrinsic acts is said [in relation] to a single [act]; and that this will is that creative potency, or eminence [eminentiam] of the essence, which is not said [in relation] to its acts; since the will is the peer [compar] of its own [suae, sc. essence].

Asphal. Ais itaque diserte voluntatem divinam ad unicum actum dici? Ubi ergo indeterminatio & determinatio ad unum ex pluribus, quae ad libertatem requiri, & in quibus collocatam esse libertatem asserebas?

Asphal. Do you say therefore expressly [diserte] that the divine will is said [in relation] to a single act? Where then [are] the indetermination and the determination to one out of more [than one], which you were asserting to be required for liberty, and in which [you were asserting] liberty to be placed?
Ereu. Prorsus affirmo, neque sustuli: tamen quae obiicis & tu quid sentias experiar. Putasne legitime concipi posse Deum existentem; sed nondum tota sua entitate perfectum & absolutum?

Ereu. I affirm [it] entirely, nor have I taken [them] away: yet I will test [experiar] both what you object and what you [yourself] think. Do you think that God can legitimately be conceived existing, but not yet perfected and absolute [absolutum] in his whole entity [entitate]?
Asphal. Palam est repugnare.
Asphal. It is plain that it is repugnant [repugnare].
Ereu. Et volitionem intrinsecam esse aliquam ipsius rationem sive partem fateris aut dubitas?
Ereu. And that the intrinsic volition is some notion [rationem] or part of him — do you confess [it] or doubt [it]?
Asphal. Fateor.
Asphal. I confess [it].

Ereu. Vides itaque haec utraque in eodem gradu confirmata esse Deum existere & ultimata volitione completum esse. Neque dubitas quin ultimata volitio caeterarum eiusdem generis & gradus exclusionem inferat. Impossibile proinde est Deum existentem indifferentem ad plures volitiones cogitare:

Ereu. You see therefore that these both are confirmed in the same degree [gradu]: that God exists, and that he is completed by the ultimate [ultimata] volition. Nor do you doubt that the ultimate volition brings in [inferat] the exclusion of the others of the same kind and degree. It is impossible accordingly to think God existing [as] indifferent to more volitions [than one]:

Quae si ad effectivam potentiam accommodes, nihil incommodi contingere vides, si vel non omnia effecerit quae potens est, vel etiam volens agere; vel si multa possit quae nunquam effecturus aut voliturus sit.

which [things], if you accommodate [them] to the effective [effectivam] potency, you see that nothing inconvenient [incommodi] happens if either he has not effected all [things] which he is able, or even willing, to do [agere]; or if he can [do] many [things] which he is never going to effect or to will.
Asphal. At nondum liquet quomodo determinabilis sit Deus qui imperfectus cogitari non potest, & iterum ad Philosophos revolvimur.
Asphal. But it is not yet clear how God may be determinable, who cannot be thought imperfect; and again we are rolled back [revolvimur] to the Philosophers.

Ereu. Quantumvis imperfectum ens a se cogitare sit nefas, illud ipsum tamen si cogitemus, non necessum est de illo quaecumque sunt in illo cogitare, neque si vellemus, permittat intellectus nostri parvitas. Possumus itaque sicut caeterorum unum non cogitato alio, sic illum aliquid volentem apprehendere, non expresso alio, quod simul velit.

Ereu. However much it be impious [nefas] to think the being from itself [ens a se] imperfect, yet if we think that very [being], it is not necessary to think of it whatever [things] are in it; nor, if we wished, would the smallness of our understanding permit [it]. We can therefore, as of the other [things] [we think] one, another not being thought, so apprehend him willing something, another [thing] not being expressed which he wills at the same time.

Apprehendimus itaque Deum sese volentem, nondum intellecto quod alia velit propter se. Hic nondum determinatum accipimus, non de ipso hoc affirmantes, sed de ipso in nostra apprehensione, ulterius respicientes videmus hanc volitionem ex ipsius ratione indifferentem ad plures mundos, sed ex adiectis aliis quae in Deo videmus, necessarium esse, ut non ab alio obiecto quam hoc quem habitamus mundo, determinabilis sit.

We apprehend therefore God willing himself, it not yet being understood that he wills other [things] for his own sake [propter se]. Here we take [him] not yet determined, not affirming this of him himself, but of him in our apprehension; looking further, we see this volition, from its own notion [ex ipsius ratione], [to be] indifferent to more worlds [than one], but from other [things] added [adiectis] which we see in God, [that] it is necessary that it be determinable by no other object than this world which we inhabit.
Et quoniam ex nostrae naturae contemplatione hunc ad Deum gradum molimur, necessarium nobis esse hunc apprehendendi & discurrendi modum, atque adeo verum, hoc est, talem qualis nobis convenit.

And since from the contemplation of our nature we labour [molimur] [to make] this step [gradum] toward God, [we see] that this mode of apprehending and discoursing [discurrendi] is necessary for us, and so [atque adeo] true, that is, such as befits us.

Et hanc solutionem puto undique evidentem, quaeque etiam pertinacissimo cuilibet os occludere abunde sufficiat, modo eam intelligat. Vos si aliter sentiatis, audire aveo; & si possim quae affertis, exhaurire: sin minus, candide manus dare.

And this solution I think evident on all sides, and [one] which would abundantly suffice to close the mouth even of any most obstinate [man], provided he understand it. You, if you think otherwise, I am eager [aveo] to hear; and, if I can, to exhaust [exhaurire] what you bring; if not, candidly to give [my] hands [manus dare].

Andab. Non ausim ego post tale solutionis praeconium neque mutire quidem, etsi alioqui satis confidens. Quoniam itaque ab hac nos contemplatione revocas, vide num etiam ego non possim aliquid huic quam texis fabricae, adminiculi conferre.

Andab. I would not dare, after such a proclamation [praeconium] of the solution, not even to mutter, though otherwise sufficiently confident. Since therefore you call us back from this contemplation, see whether I too may not be able to contribute something of prop [adminiculi] to this fabric [fabricae] which you are weaving.

[Margin, p. 341: Deum esse gubernatorem mundi.] Certe dum Deum intelligentem esse conficeres, visum est mihi eodem argumento constare posse etiam omniscientem esse: Cum enim omnia ab eo procedant, necessum est etiam omnia in eo inesse seu contineri: procedunt enim ab ipso solo sine adminiculo alterius alicuius causae: Unde in eo plene & perfecte praehaberi fit.

[Margin, p. 341: That God is the governor of the world.] Certainly, while you were concluding [conficeres] that God is intelligent, it seemed to me that by the same argument it could be established that he is also omniscient: for since all [things] proceed from him, it is necessary also that all [things] be in [inesse] him, or be contained [in him]; for they proceed from him alone without the prop [adminiculo] of some other cause: whence it comes about [fit] [that they] are pre-had [praehaberi] in him fully and perfectly.

Si itaque idem est in Deo inexistere secundum suam proprietatem & distinctionem, atque cognosci, omnia a Deo cognosci asserendum est: & quandoquidem Essentia Dei & proinde cognitio infinitae sunt, sequitur cognitionem ipsius non ad res dumtaxat, verum etiam ad omnes earum coniugationes & coniugationum effecta, & singulas horum circumstantias adeo nullo labore, motu vel molestia ferri, ut neque pulvisculus in duo dirimatur, neque capillus in terram decidat, sine ipsius cognitione, immo sine ipsius ordine & approbatione:

If therefore it is the same in God to be in [inexistere] [him] according to its [own] property and distinction, and to be known, it must be asserted that all [things] are known by God; and since the Essence of God, and accordingly [his] knowledge [cognitio], are infinite, it follows that his knowledge is borne [ferri] not to things only, but also to all their conjugations [coniugationes] and the effects of the conjugations, and the single circumstances of these, with so [adeo] no labour, motion or trouble, that neither is a little particle of dust [pulvisculus] divided in two, nor does a hair fall to the earth, without his knowledge — nay, without his order and approbation:

quandoquidem qui effecta videt causarum quas ipse facit, si adaequate ex iis causis fluunt, non potest non ipsa effecta velle. Nihil itaque per totum universum tam leve, tam nihili est, quod non a Deo praecognitum, praevolitum, praeordinatum, praeeffectum sit.

since he who sees the effects of the causes which he himself makes, if they flow adequately [adaequate] from those causes, cannot not will the effects themselves. Nothing therefore through the whole universe is so light, so of nothing [nihili], that it is not foreknown, forewilled, foreordained, foreeffected [praeeffectum] by God.

Unde etiam haec constant; neque deficere posse quicquid ipse efficaciter vult & intendit: neque quicquam praeter ipsius voluntatem geri, nedum contra vel ut quicquam ei resistat. Habemus ergo, nisi quid me in hac deductione latuerit, Deum universi cui eum conditorem nobis dederas, etiam gubernatorem & praefectum.

Whence also these [things] stand established [constant]: neither can whatever he efficaciously wills and intends fail; nor is anything done [geri] besides his will, much less against [it], or so that anything resist him. We have therefore, unless something has lain hidden from me in this deduction, God — whom you had given us [as] founder [conditorem] for the universe [universi cui] — also [as] its governor and prefect [praefectum].

Ereu. Ego vero nihil calumnior in hac dissertatione, licet enim videam quae contra afferri possint, eiusmodi tamen sunt quae maiorem potius explicationem flagitent quam quae veritati dictorum obstent.

Ereu. I indeed make no false charge [nihil calumnior] in this dissertation; for although I see what may be brought against [it], yet they are of such a kind as demand a greater explication rather than such as stand in the way of the truth of [the things] said.

Quoniam vero abstractionis Metaphysicae sunt & originem naturamque scientiae & cognitionis tangunt, & extranea sunt ab his quae nostro coetu hactenus persecuti sumus, praetermittenda ea & posthabenda tuis laudibus qui tam disertam nobis gubernationis divinae demonstrationem patefecisti, arbitror.

But since they are of Metaphysical abstraction, and touch the origin and nature of science [scientiae] and knowledge [cognitionis], and are foreign [extranea] from those [things] which we have pursued hitherto in our gathering [coetu], I judge [arbitror] that they are to be passed over and placed after [posthabenda] your praises, [you] who have laid open to us so eloquent [disertam] a demonstration of the divine government.

terms: mutatio = actual change; mutabilitas = ‘possibility of act in the mutable’ (Ereunius’ definition, p. 337).
The Knot’s thesis: God’s power to found another world does not make Him mutable; White defines mutability as a real possibility of a new act, which he denies in God.
potentia / actus / in potentia / exire in actum
potency / act / in potency / go out into act
potentia also ‘power’; exitus in actum = ‘going-out into act’.
Aristotelian act–potency pair; White argues God’s ‘potency’ is said only by analogy (p. 338).
Plurality of possible objects vs. the single act that ‘sates’ an elective power.
White’s image for an elective power: its whole capacity is fulfilled by one choice.
Scholastic: powers that choose one among several; the axiom ‘frustra potentia quae nunquam reducitur ad actum’ fails in them.
the object or end-point at which an act ends; ‘term’ also = logical term.
Scholastic: an act is ‘terminated’ at its object; Andabata makes creation only an extrinsic termination of God’s eternal love.
effective willing vs. God’s general love of all possibles.
Andabata’s (Thomist-style) view that the decree to create adds nothing intrinsic to God.
prior in the order of causes, not of time.
Scholastic priority of nature: cause before effect even when simultaneous.
equivocal by design, i.e. analogical naming.
Boethian division of equivocals a casu / a consilio; White says ‘potentia’ is said of God by analogy (cf. glossary, D1).
be predicated relatively of; ‘be directed to’.
Category of relation (πρός τι): God is not ‘said in relation to’ any act outside Himself.
Ereunius: God is ‘completed’ by His ultimate volition, so an existent God cannot be indifferent to several volitions.
Here mostly the formal concept (‘ratio potentiae’, ‘ex ipsius ratione’), rendered ‘notion’ per the glossary.
White’s name for God established earlier in Dialogue III.
Uncertain sense: a man who has the art ready but need not use it.
stupid; ‘the bearded’ = philosophers (cf. Horace/Persius’ bearded sage).
Comic jibes at the Philosophers as in D3-N05.
Scholastic: the effects pre-exist (‘praehaberi’) in their cause; to be in God is to be known by Him.
White’s term for concurrences of causes and their joint effects.
neque pulvisculus … neque capillus in terram decidat
neither a little particle of dust … nor a hair falls to the earth
Allusion to Matthew 10:29–30 / Luke 21:18 (sparrow and the numbered hairs), the classic proof-text of particular providence.
Climactic series of the doctrine of providence; the margin heads the passage ‘Deum esse gubernatorem mundi’.
Andabata adds the ‘governing cause’ (causa gubernans) to the founding cause; cf. the four causes of the work’s title.
Classical idiom (Caesar, Cicero) for conceding defeat.
to toast, offer a drink; ‘neat’ (unmixed) wine.
Sympotic metaphor: Andabata invites a purer draught of argument.
Alexander’s knot, picking up Ereunius’ ‘nodi sectura’ at the end of Knot viii.
The interlocutors’ conversation as a circle of friends.
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot ix (complete). PDF pp. 344–354 = printed pp. 333–343, from Andabata’s ‘Non eam inficias esse nodum vere Gordianum’ (p. 333, margin ‘Nodus IX’) to Ereunius’ ‘…demonstrationem patefecisti, arbitror.’ (p. 343). Offset +11 holds (p. 343 = PDF 354). Signatures Tt iij (p. 333), Vu (p. 337), Vu ij (p. 339), Vu iij (p. 341).

Following the book, not the table: the Syllogismus gives 335 for Knot ix, but the margin places it on p. 333 (as noted in D3-N08). Knot x (‘Fundamentum fati Stoicorum’, table p. 343) has its margin on p. 343 beside the middle of Asphalius’ speech (‘Ereuni, utrique vestrum me oppono. Et quoniam alter Deum conditorem…’). This Knot is ended at the preceding speaker break; Knot x begins with Asphalius’ ‘Ego vero reclamo huic iniquae duorum consensioni’ (PDF 354). The margin on p. 341 ‘Deum esse gubernatorem mundi’ is a topic note inside Knot ix, not a new Knot.

Uncertain readings and constructions: (1) p. 333 ‘distinuisse’ — clearly printed so (checked at 300 dpi); not a Latin word; taken as a misprint for ‘detinuisse’ (held), marked {?distinuisse}. (2) p. 337 ‘homo explicatus’ — sense uncertain (‘accomplished’, ‘unencumbered’); the point is a man who possesses an art without using it. (3) p. 335 ‘etsi potuit non esse’ — read as ‘et si’, since concessive ‘although’ gives no sense. (4) p. 339 ‘cum voluntas suae compar sit’ — elliptical; ‘suae [essentiae]’ understood. (5) p. 338 ‘Deus autem potentia … nominatur’ — potentia taken as ablative (named by [the name of] potency). (6) p. 342 ‘Deum universi cui eum conditorem nobis dederas’ — cui taken with universi (‘for the universe’); the construction is loose. (7) p. 334 ‘Acute, Ita me Deus amet … sed quod … prodidisti’ — read as praise qualified: sharp, but only what one could expect of Andabata without a miracle. (8) p. 335 ‘putasne … sunt.’ is printed with a full stop; translated as a question. No illegible readings.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images (p. 333 and p. 337 zoomed at 300 dpi) and against the English. The check produced 4 corrections: (i) p. 340 ‘vel etiam volens agere’ — first drafted as a separate clause (‘or even willing to act’); corrected so that potens and volens both govern agere (‘which he is able, or even willing, to do’); (ii) p. 338 ‘aequivocationem ex consilio’ — first drafted ‘purposely call equivocation’; corrected to the glossary’s technical ‘equivocation from deliberation’ (ex consilio qualifies the noun, Boethian a consilio); (iii) p. 334 ‘Extrinsecam … terminationem … inducere’ — the accusative-infinitive restructured so that the termination is subject of ‘induces’ and ‘suspect’ governs it; (iv) p. 338 ‘ratio potentiae’ — first drafted ‘reason’, changed to ‘notion’ per the glossary (ratio as concept).

Conventions: as in previous units (see glossary.md). Long speeches are split at sense-breaks (continuation rows carry no speaker head). plura = more [things]; potentia = potency; dici ad = be said in relation to; terminatio = termination; ratio (concept) = notion.
